blocks.content: One of the most important and debated questions in OOP and domain design: should your objects just hold data, or should they also know how to behave? The answer shapes everything code structure, testability, maintainability, and how clearly your code reflects the business.
1. The Core Question
In object-oriented programming, every object can have two things: data (fields) and behaviour(methods). The question is: how much should a domain object know about what it can do?
This diagram compares two ways of designing domain objects: the Anemic Domain Model and the Rich Domain Model. The Rich Domain Model is the approach encouraged by Domain-Driven Design (DDD).
1. Anemic Domain Model
In an Anemic Domain Model, objects only contain data. They have fields, getters, and setters, but very little or no business behavior.
In the diagram, the Order class only stores data such as id, status, and total. Operations like cancelOrder(), shipOrder(), and calculateTotal() are placed inside a separate OrderService.
As a result, business logic becomes scattered across multiple service classes, while domain objects become simple data containers.
The key problem is:
The object knows its data but doesn't know how to use it.
2. Rich Domain Model
In a Rich Domain Model, objects contain both data and behavior.
In the diagram, the Order object not only stores id, status, and total, but also contains methods such as cancel(), ship(), and calculateTotal().
These methods enforce business rules directly inside the object. For example, the cancel() method can check whether the order has already been shipped before allowing cancellation.
The key idea is:
The object owns both its data and the business rules related to that data.
Services become much thinner and mainly coordinate between objects rather than containing all the business logic.
ORIGIN OF THE TERM

Martin Fowler coined "Anemic Domain Model" in 2003 and called it an anti-pattern a violation of the basic principles of OOP. The irony is that it's also the most common pattern in enterprise Java, often baked in by frameworks that encourage separating data classes from service classes.
2. What is an Anemic Domain Model?
blocks.text: 2. What is an Anemic Domain Model?

blocks.content: An anemic domain model has classes that look like domain objects they have the right names (Order, Customer, Product) but they contain almost nothing except fields and getters/setters. Every piece of logic lives in a separate service class.

ANALOGY: A PUPPET WITH NO STRINGS

Imagine a puppet that can only be posed by an external puppeteer it has no ability to move on its own. Every action requires the puppeteer to reach in and manually manipulate it. 

The puppet has shape (data) but no agency (behaviour). An anemic model is that puppet it has structure but no intelligence. The services are the puppeteers.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: This looks organised everything in one service. But it has deep problems that only become visible as the codebase grows.
3. What is a Rich Domain Model?
blocks.text: 3. What is a Rich Domain Model?

blocks.content: A rich domain model puts behaviour where it belongs inside the objects that own the data. An Order object knows how to cancel itself, how to add items, how to validate its own state. Services exist only to coordinate between objects, not to make all the decisions for them.

ANALOGY: A SELF-DRIVING CAR VS A REMOTE-CONTROLLED CAR

A remote-controlled car relies entirely on an external operator to decide every move turn left, accelerate, brake. That's anemic. A self-driving car has its own intelligence: it knows the rules of the road, it detects obstacles, it makes its own decisions. The driver (service) tells it the destination the car handles how. That's a rich model.

blocks.content: 4. Side-by-Side Code Comparison
The same business requirement "cancel an order only if it hasn't been shipped" implemented both ways. Watch how different they feel.

["Requirement: Cancel an order. 
","Rules: cannot cancel if shipped or delivered.
"]
items: Rules: cannot cancel if shipped or delivered.

blocks.content: ANEMIC: RULE BURIED INSIDE A SERVICE, OBJECT HAS NO SAY
RICH: RULE LIVES INSIDE ORDER, ENFORCED EVERYWHERE AUTOMATICALLY
In the rich model, the service becomes a thin orchestrator. It loads the object, calls its method, saves the result. The decision whether the cancel is valid is made by the Order, not the service.
This diagram shows that the Order object is responsible for enforcing its own business rules and controlling how its state changes over time.

An order goes through different stages during its lifecycle. It starts in the Draft state, moves to Placed when the customer confirms it, then to Shipped when it leaves the warehouse, and finally to Delivered when it reaches the customer.
The key idea is that the Order itself knows which state transitions are valid. It understands that a Draft order can be placed, a Placed order can be shipped, and a Shipped order can be delivered.

The red dashed line represents the cancellation rule. An order can be cancelled only before it is shipped. Once the order reaches the Shipped or Delivered state, cancellation is no longer allowed. The Order object enforces this rule itself.

In a Rich Domain Model, the service layer does not decide whether an order can be cancelled. The service simply asks the Order to perform the action. The Order then checks its current state and determines whether the operation is valid.

This keeps business rules inside the domain object where they belong. As a result, the Order becomes the single source of truth for its lifecycle, making the system easier to understand, maintain, and extend.
In simple terms:
The Order does not just store its status; it understands what that status means and what actions are allowed next. That is what makes it a Rich Domain Model.
5. Where Business Logic Lives
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1780818471868-608562465.png

On the left side, the Order, Customer, and Product objects contain mostly data, while a Massive Service Layercontains all the business rules. As the application grows, this service layer becomes larger and larger because every rule is added there.
The result is a service that knows everything about orders, customers, and products, making it difficult to maintain.
On the right side, the business logic is moved into a Rich Domain Model. Each object becomes responsible for its own rules.
The Order knows how to cancel itself, the Customer knows whether it is eligible for a feature, and the Product knows whether a discount can be applied.
Instead of one huge service making all decisions, each domain object owns the rules related to its own data. This keeps logic organized, reduces complexity, and makes the system easier to understand.
In simple terms:
Bad design: Objects store data, services contain all logic.
Good design: Objects store data and the business rules that operate on that data.
That's the core idea behind a Rich Domain Model in Domain-Driven Design
6. Problems with Anemic Models
Problem 1: Rules can be bypassed
If an Order has a public setStatus(), any code anywhere in the codebase can directly set any status.
A new developer writes order.setStatus("CANCELLED") without knowing the business rules. The rule "can't cancel a shipped order" is violated silently.
NOTHING PREVENTS THIS BYPASS

order.setStatus("CANCELLED"); // bypasses all rules in OrderService
orderRepo.save(order);         // shipped order is now marked cancelled — data corrupted

blocks.content: Problem 2: Duplicate logic across services

The cancellation rule exists in OrderService.cancelOrder(). Then a refund flow is added in RefundService it also needs to check if the order can be cancelled. Now the rule is in two places. They drift apart. One gets updated, the other doesn't. Bugs follow.
Problem 3: Services become god classes

All logic gravitates to services. OrderService starts with 5 methods and ends up with 50. It handles cancellation, shipping, pricing, discounts, returns, notifications, tax, analytics. It becomes impossible to understand or safely modify. Testing requires mocking a dozen dependencies.
HOW ORDERSERVICE GROWS IN AN ANEMIC CODEBASE
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1780818472760-422735747.png
Problem 4: OOP in name only
You're using Java classes and objects, but the design is fundamentally procedural. The classes are just structs. The services are just functions.
You get all the complexity of OOP (the object graph, the dependencies, the inheritance) with none of the benefit (encapsulation, cohesion, self-documenting behaviour).

The anemic model is seductive because it looks clean at first. "Separation of data and logic" sounds like a good principle. But the real principle of OOP is encapsulation  data and the behaviour that operates on it belong together. Splitting them apart violates the core reason objects exist.
7. Benefits of Rich Domain Models
Rich Domain Models keep business logic inside domain objects instead of scattering it across service classes. This leads to cleaner, safer, and more maintainable code.
Benefit 1: Rules Are Enforced Everywhere

When business rules are implemented inside the domain object, every operation automatically follows those rules. For example, if cancellation logic lives inside the Order object, every cancellation request must go through the same validation process. This prevents rule bypasses and ensures there is a single place to maintain the business logic.
Benefit 2: Self-Documenting Code

Rich domain models make the code easier to understand because the available actions are exposed directly by the object. Looking at an Order object immediately tells you what operations can be performed on it. This makes the domain model closely reflect the business language and improves readability.
Benefit 3: Easier Unit Testing

Since business logic resides inside domain objects, those objects can be tested independently without requiring databases, frameworks, or external dependencies. Tests become simpler, faster, and more focused on validating business behavior rather than application setup.
Benefit 4: Thin and Focused Services

When domain objects handle business rules, services no longer need to contain complex logic. Their responsibility becomes coordinating the workflow, such as loading data, invoking domain methods, saving changes, and publishing events. This keeps services small, easy to understand, and easier to maintain.
8. When Anemic is Actually Fine
Rich domain models are not always the right choice. There are legitimate scenarios where anemic models are appropriate and pragmatic.
THE REAL SIGNAL
Use a rich model when your domain has complex business rules, state transitions, or invariants that need to be enforced consistently.

If you're writing validation logic in multiple services, if services are growing massive, or if bugs keep appearing because rules were applied inconsistently those are all signs you need a richer model.
9. Migrating from Anemic to Rich
Most real codebases start anemic and grow into problems. Here's a practical, step-by-step approach to migrating without rewriting everything at once.
Step 1: Stop adding new setters
For any new field, don't add a setter. Add a meaningful method instead. setStatus("CANCELLED") → cancel(). This is the smallest possible change and immediately starts moving in the right direction.
Step 2: Move logic from services into objects, one rule at a time
Step 3: Replace string status with an enum
Step 4: Make invalid states unrepresentable

Use the type system to prevent impossible states. If an order can't exist without items, enforce that in the constructor. If total must always equal the sum of items, make setTotal() private and recalculate automatically when items change.
Step 5: Replace service method logic with object method calls
Once rules are in the objects, the service methods shrink to 3–5 lines. A service that loads, calls, saves, and emits an event is the ideal end state.

You don't have to migrate everything at once. Start with the most bug-prone part of your system usually where rules are duplicated or where services have grown largest. Move one rule into the domain object, write a pure unit test for it, delete the corresponding service logic. Repeat.
10. Summary

["Anemic domain model: objects hold only data fields and getters/setters. All business logic lives in service classes. Objects know nothing about what they can do.","Rich domain model: objects hold data AND behaviour. Business rules live inside the objects they apply to. Use anemic when it's genuinely just CRUD with no domain logic.","Migrate gradually: stop adding setters, move one rule at a time into domain objects, use enums over strings, make invalid states unrepresentable.","The goal: services become thin orchestrators (3–10 lines). items: Anemic domain model: objects hold only data fields and getters/setters. All business logic lives in service classes. Objects know nothing about what they can do.
Rich domain model: objects hold data AND behaviour. Business rules live inside the objects they apply to. Services only orchestrate load, call, save, emit.
Anemic models look clean early but become unmaintainable services grow into god classes, rules get duplicated, and state can be bypassed through setters.
Rich models make rules impossible to bypass the only way to cancel an order is through order.cancel(), which enforces the rule every time, everywhere.
Rich domain objects are easier to unit test a pure new Order().cancel() test needs no mocks, no Spring context, no database setup.
Use rich models when the domain has complex rules, state transitions, or invariants. Use anemic when it's genuinely just CRUD with no domain logic.
Migrate gradually: stop adding setters, move one rule at a time into domain objects, use enums over strings, make invalid states unrepresentable.
The goal: services become thin orchestrators (3–10 lines). Domain objects become self-documenting, self-protecting, independently testable.
